extracted.intended_audience: poets, critics, and students of poetry; readers seeking principles for evaluating or composing poems
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts critical criteria for judging and producing poetry: definitions of a poem, necessary qualities of poetic genius, and practical standards of diction, metre, imagery, and intellectual depth, illustrated by analyses of Shakespeare, Wordsworth, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: poem's immediate object is pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem is that species of composition which is opposed to works of science by proposing for its immediate object pleasure, not truth; and from all other species it is discriminated by proposing to itself such delight from the whole, as is compatible with a distinct gratification from each component part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes poetry by purpose (pleasure) and by requiring that each part contribute distinct gratification. Examples/contrast: works of science aim at truth; novels and romances may aim for pleasure but must justify poetic form if metre is superadded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superficial form: metre and rhyme as poetic charm
rubrics_metrics.description: All compositions that have the charm of anticipating recurrence of sounds and quantities (metre and rhyme) may be entitled poems in this lowest sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that metre/rhyme alone can produce pleasure; but warns this is only 'superficial form' — true poetry requires deeper unity and appropriateness of parts to metrical arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and mutual support of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate poem must be one the parts of which mutually support and explain each other; all in their proportion harmonizing with, and supporting the purpose and known influences of metrical arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: series of striking lines or distiches each absorbing attention and forming separate wholes; unsustained compositions where reader only collects a rapid general result. The poem should carry the reader forward by the pleasure of the journey, not just mechanical curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement: pleasurable activity of mind throughout
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader should be carried forward, not merely by mechanical impulse of curiosity to arrive at a solution, but by the pleasurable activity of mind excited by the attractions of the journey itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems should provide continuing attractions at every step; the movement should create forward momentum balanced with moments of reflection (analogy: serpent motion or path of sound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Studied selection and artificial arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: To produce a harmonious whole, the remaining parts must be preserved in keeping with the poetry by such a studied selection and artificial arrangement as will excite more continuous and equal attention than prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition requires conscious arrangement—selecting and ordering parts so each contributes to overall poetic attention and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic Imagination: synthesis of opposites
rubrics_metrics.description: The Imagination reveals itself in the balance or reconcilement of opposite or discordant qualities: of sameness with difference; of the general with the concrete; the idea with the image; the individual with the representative; novelty with the familiar; judgment with enthusiasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination is the synthetic power that fuses faculties, subordinating art to nature and manner to matter; it's the central faculty distinguishing a true poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite faculties: good sense, fancy, motion, imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Sense is the Body of poetic genius, Fancy its Drapery, Motion its Life, and Imagination the Soul that is everywhere and in each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes balance: sound judgment, ornament (fancy), dynamism (motion), and unifying imagination all necessary for poetic genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification and musical sweetness
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect sweetness of the versification; its adaptation to the subject; and the power displayed in varying the march of the words without passing into a loftier and more majestic rhythm than is demanded by the thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delight in richness and sweetness of sound, when evidently original (not mechanical imitation), is a strong promise of poetic genius. The poet must vary rhythm appropriately to subject; musicality should be intrinsic, not merely an imitable mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of subject: remoteness from personal circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: A promise of genius is the choice of subjects very remote from the private interests and circumstances of the writer himself; when the subject is immediately from the author’s personal sensations, excellence may be an equivocal and fallacious pledge of genuine poetic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great poets can render characters and situations beyond their personal experience; excessive autobiographical subjects risk mistaking cultivated skill for innate genius (example: Venus and Adonis shows aloof, analytical presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery must be vivified by passion or thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Images become proofs of original genius only as far as they are modified by a predominant passion; or by associated thoughts or images awakened by that passion; or when they have the effect of reducing multitude to unity, or succession to an instant; or when a human and intellectual life is transferred to them from the poet’s own spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely beautiful, faithfully copied images do not suffice; imagery must be integrated with feeling and intellect to become truly poetic. Example contrast provided with alternate phrasings turning prosaic description into poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery of simultaneity (succession rendered simultaneous)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should supply the liveliest image of succession with the feeling of simultaneousness (e.g., motions and transitions rendered as immediate, vivid images).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: compress succession into an instant of feeling or image so the reader experiences movement and simultaneity together (illustrated by Shakespearean lines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and energy of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth, and energy of thought: no man was ever yet a great poet without being at the same time a profound philosopher. Poetry is the blossom and the fragrancy of all human knowledge, human thoughts, human passions, emotions, language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry requires intellectual seriousness—knowledge and reflection wedded to feeling. Without depth, poetic talent risks being meteoric and transitory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: purity, appropriateness, and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard the purity of the native tongue; avoid words which a gentleman would not use in dignified conversation or words only a learned man would use. Language is the armoury of the human mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: meretricious, over-worn finery; obscure, enigmatic expression; using pompous or learned words that obscure meaning. The best diction is appropriate, plain where necessary, and preserves native idiom (citing Dante's injunctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical craftsmanship and subtle balances of sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater variety and more charming effect arise from countless modifications and subtle balances of sound in the common metres of their country, rather than from introduced mechanical metres with overpowering tunes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer delicate, intelligent variations within natural metre to foreign or forcible metrical experiments that impose an external tune and distract from meaning (criticizes some modern imported metres).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overemphasis on novelty at expense of finish
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern poets often propose new and striking images and specific incidents but are comparatively careless in diction and metre; earlier poets sought superior excellence in manner of treating the same subjects (polish and simplicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal is a union: recall high finish, appropriateness, facility and omnipresent grace of earlier poets combined with the keener interest, deeper pathos, and fresher imagery of moderns. Anti-patterns: novelty for its own sake with careless form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of real life (Wordsworth's experiment) — contested scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordsworth presented an experiment whether subjects that naturally reject usual ornaments might be managed in the language of ordinary life to produce pleasurable interest; he was understood to contend for extending this style to poetry generally, which sparked controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges value in plain, real-life language for some poetry but warns against treating 'language of real life' as a universal rule; Hazlitt concedes some points but objects to extending it dogmatically to all poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between image/incident and metrical/diction craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither striking images nor incidents alone secure poetic praise if diction and metrical arrangement are neglected; likewise exquisite polish without imaginative substance is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: poets who focus solely on new subjects and portrait-like specificity but neglect metrical principle and diction produce work of uneven merit. The poet should combine subject-matter interest with craft in diction and metre.
